name: Inversion
originator: Carl Jacobi (maths); Charlie Munger (popularised); Gary Klein (pre-mortem, 2007)
rule: Ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid it. Or imagine the project has already failed and ask why.
plain: Instead of 'how do we succeed?', ask 'how would we fail?' The answers are easier to see.

story.beat: The rescue plan is ready. Before the vote, you ask everyone: 'It's 90 days from now. The colony ran out of air. Write down why.' The answers: the backup pump was never tested, one person held all the fungicide codes, and nobody watched the sensor at night. Three holes, found in ten minutes, fixed before they mattered.

examples.text: 'How would we guarantee a medication error?' Similar labels on two drugs. Relabel them.
'How could landing go wrong?' Nobody checks the pad for debris. Add a checklist item.
'How would I make sure I never exercise?' Keep the gear in storage. So keep it by the door.

settings.prompt: It's day 90. We ran out of air. Why?

realCase.title: Space Shuttle Challenger
realCase.text: The night before launch, engineers warned that cold weather could stop the rubber O-ring seals working and argued for delay. Managers asked them to prove it was unsafe rather than asking what would make it fail. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch.
realCase.source: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission, 1986)

misuse: Listing every imaginable failure until nothing ever launches. Rank failure modes by likelihood and impact, then act.
sources: Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', Harvard Business Review (Sept 2007)

predict.prompt: Which question finds hidden risks in a plan fastest?
predict.why: A pre-mortem makes it safe to name failure modes.

mcq.prompt: At Challenger, the burden of proof was put on…
mcq.why: Inverted the wrong way: 'prove it will fail' instead of 'show it won't'.

whichModel.prompt: Before a product launch, a team writes the imaginary headline 'Launch disaster' and lists the causes.
